items.title: ObservabilityCON 2026: A guide to all the announcements from Grafana Labs
items.summary: Today at ObservabilityCON 2026 in San Francisco, we unveiled a range of new Grafana Cloud capabilities designed to reshape cloud economics, bring richer context and deeper visibility across your systems and end-user experiences, and help teams move toward autonomous operations.Check out the keynote to learn more about the latest updates to the open agentic observability cloud, and read on for a quick recap of all the news from ObservabilityCON 2026.Autonomous operations with the help of AIWith Grafana Assistant in Grafana Cloud, you can bring more of your operational tasks together in one place so you can resolve incidents faster and get back to building. And you're doing it with AI features that automate much of the undifferentiated heavy lifting while still keeping you in control. Assistant Investigations, generally available since late July, lets you run longer, deeper investigations that can start automatically from an alert or incident, and teams can run them from the platform, Slack, the Grafana Cloud MCP server, or gcx. And today we're adding new AI features to help you take your automation even further:Assistant Watchers (now generally available) are always-on agents that detect changes not captured by predefined alert rules. You describe what to monitor in plain language and select the relevant data sources. Your watcher then establishes a baseline from historical telemetry patterns and surfaces findings when those patterns change. Grafana Managed Sandboxes (public preview) gives you a controlled cloud environment to ask questions about source code, make changes, and prepare pull requests from conversations in Grafana Cloud. It uses context from your repository code and live telemetry to propose potential fixes within a sandbox environment that a person on your team can then review and approve. Grafana Pages (public preview) lets you build visualizations beyond any fixed constraints, making them closer to an app than a dashboard. You describe what you need, and Assistant builds a page in the canvas—all without you having to write any code. Existing visualization components still work, and Pages supplement them as the next evolution of Grafana. With Grafana Cloud, you decide which parts of your operations you want to handle manually and which parts you want to hand off to Assistant.To learn more about how you can get the most out of Grafana Cloud's AI capabilities, check out our blog posts on autonomous operations and Pages.Cloud economics reimagined  In the AI era, where teams are managing more telemetry than ever, they need to be able to find the right log line in seconds. They also need to know they're only storing the telemetry that's worth paying for. That's why we're making major query performance enhancements to Grafana Cloud Logs, built on technology from our Logline acquisition, and giving you more precision with Adaptive Telemetry, so your costs scale with the value you get from your data.Keep only the data worth paying for: Adaptive Telemetry updatesGrafana Labs’ Adaptive Telemetry suite optimizes cost across metrics, logs, traces, and profiles by recommending what to aggregate or sample, so teams keep the telemetry that matters. Customers have cut telemetry spend by 30% to 50% on average. “Moving to Grafana Cloud and using Adaptive Telemetry cut our metrics costs enough to fund logs and traces as well," says Carl Eastman, Principal Software Engineer, Rapid7. "Our visibility went up while our costs went down, and dashboards and queries are faster and less noisy.” New updates cover logs, metrics, and traces:Adaptive Metrics auto-apply (generally available) continuously applies recommendations, while existing dashboards and alerts keep working unchanged. With cost-first mode, a built-in safeguard only applies recommendations that won’t increase your total active series, so optimization never turns into a cost spike.Adaptive Logs Archive (public preview) routes logs to an object storage bucket you own. Get the cost savings from not putting those logs in Grafana Cloud, but make sure they still exist in low-cost storage for investigations, audits, or compliance requests. And with Adaptive Logs replay (sign up for the private preview), you can bring those logs back on demand.Query traces dropped by Adaptive Traces (generally available) to sample aggressively without worrying about losing the one trace you need. Retrieve any trace by ID from the last 24 hours, even if Adaptive Traces dropped it, so cost savings never come at the expense of an investigation.Volumetric sampling (generally available) gives you a more valuable sample than probabilistic sampling. It spreads your sampling budget fairly across services and request types, so low-volume services aren't crowded out. It also adjusts as your traffic changes. items.title: From production problem to proposed fix: Implement autonomous operations with Grafana AI
items.summary: You've just finished a deployment, and though your service is up, you start to notice some requests are getting slower. To address the lag, someone—or, more likely, some group of people on your team—needs to watch the dashboards, decide whether the change matters, investigate what happened, and turn the findings into a fix. At each step you're gathering context—and often explaining that context again to the next person or tool. To make matters worse for the team responsible for the service, all this work is getting in the way of everything else they need to build. With Grafana Assistant in Grafana Cloud, you can bring more of those tasks together in one place, helping you resolve incidents faster so you can get back to building. And you're doing it with AI features that automate much of the undifferentiated heavy lifting while still keeping you in control. Assistant Watchers (generally available today as part of ObservabilityCON 2026) provides ongoing attention to the conditions you care about. Assistant Investigations (generally available) gathers evidence about what changed. And Grafana Managed Sandboxes (public preview as of today) uses that context to prepare changes in a controlled cloud environment, giving your team something concrete to review. In this blog post, I'll show you how you can use these features collectively for better observability outcomes.Give the service ongoing attentionConsider a checkout service after a release. You want to know whether customers are encountering sustained errors or slower responses, while also accounting for the brief disruption you expect during deployment. With Watchers, our always-on agents, you describe that concern and select the relevant data sources. Assistant then analyzes your historical telemetry to establish a baseline and calibrate the checks. From there, the watcher periodically assesses those signals and provides reporting along with the evidence behind its findings. If a watcher finds a critical issue, it can automatically start an investigation with Investigations, our agent designed to help you go really deep into your incidents. That way, you can delegate recurring health checks to Assistant so your team can focus on other tasks instead. Existing alerts continue to cover known conditions that require dependable paging, while the watcher adds contextual assessment around the service. The best part: With support for Google BigQuery alongside operational telemetry sources, your watchers aren't limited to traditional observability scenarios. They can also monitor business signals, helping your entire organization keep tabs on critical changes that could impact the bottom line.Start investigating with the evidence attachedOf course, a notification is just the beginning of the response. The next questions are familiar: Which requests are affected? When did the behavior change? Is the database involved, or is another dependency slowing down?Investigations can explore metrics, logs, traces, and profiles, test hypotheses, and assemble findings with supporting source queries. From there, your responders can inspect the evidence and steer the investigation as they learn more.In our checkout example, suppose the evidence points toward repeated database calls in a request path. The useful handoff to a developer now includes the affected service, the symptoms, and the evidence supporting that hypothesis. The user has a starting point for checking the code.Turn the findings into a proposed changeManaged Sandboxes, which give Assistant a controlled cloud environment to develop proposed fixes using repository code and live telemetry, carry that investigation context into your codebase. With the relevant repository connected and coding enabled, an agent can inspect the code, prepare changes, and run available checks in a Grafana sandbox.For our example, the task could be to examine the database access pattern, prepare a targeted change, and add a regression test. Managed Sandboxes' repository-specific environments can provide the tools and dependencies needed to build and test the project. The goal should be for Assistant to deliver a proposed pull request that the team can evaluate: what changed, why it addresses the suspected cause, which checks ran, and what still needs verification. So when you respond, the investigation is already underway, with supporting telemetry and, as the workflow progresses, a proposed fix to review.Keep the decisions visible, and stay in controlA passing test is useful evidence, but your team still needs to confirm recovery in production as part of its release process. Your reviewers need to decide whether the diagnosis fits, whether the proposed change is appropriate, and how to deploy it. After rollout, they can use production telemetry to check the outcome and keep monitoring for recurrence.That makes autonomy practical: delegate recurring observation, evidence gathering, and preparation of changes, while retaining clear decisions

items.title: Grafana Pages: Turn data into interactive experiences with the next evolution of Grafana
items.summary: Teams often spend as much time preparing information as discussing it: gathering charts, checking business reports, and finding the GitHub activity that explains a change. Every follow-up question can lead to yet another round of work. That's why, as part of ObservabilityCON 2026, we're excited to introduce Grafana Pages, a new feature in Grafana Cloud that gives you a canvas to describe what you need and build a live app in minutes, based on your real data, context, and interactions. From new types of visualizations to slides and even to games, the only limitation is your imagination.With Pages, currently in public preview, you can create interactive views and tools with Grafana Assistant, using the data you already access through Grafana. There's no code and no setup; no export, upload, or deploy steps. Unlike standard dashboards, which are fixed grids of panels, you simply describe what you need, refine it through conversation, and share it with your team to explore and return to as needed.What Pages unlocksPages let you build trusted, reliable, and scalable (mini) apps in the environment you know and use with Grafana Assistant by your side. Oftentimes, broad solutions might miss a use case that’s specific to your organization. But with Pages you can easily build and own your own information hub, whether it's an incident view, a runbook, a deploy tracker, an exec readout, or a customer-facing status page.Let's look at some ways you can build Pages today.Build on your existing data connectionsGetting an internal tool working starts with connecting it to useful data. Pages builds on the data connections you already use in Grafana, giving you a starting point for bringing operational and business information together.Put transaction volumes beside service performance, or build a release review around production trends and relevant connected context. Spend your effort shaping the experience around the question your team needs to answer, rather than getting bogged down trying to figure out all the visualization bells and whistles.Let colleagues answer the next questionA shared view often leads to other questions you hadn't initially considered. One person might want to know about impacts on a specific region. A second might ask when the issue started, while a third wants to know which service is driving the change.Pages can include filters, time-range controls, and drilldowns so colleagues can explore those questions themselves. Start with an overview, narrow it to a region or service, and inspect the supporting detail—all without asking someone to prepare another report.Reuse the work; take the idea furtherBuild a page once, then return to it with a new time range for the next review. Refine it through Assistant as your team discovers which comparisons and details matter.The remix feature in Pages gives a good idea room to grow. A colleague might build a useful deployment tracker; you might see how to extend it into a broader release review. Start from their Page, add your perspective, and turn it into something neither of you had to build from scratch.Trust what you seeA page is only useful if people believe it. Every page keeps its sources, which are the queries behind each chart and number, so you and your colleagues can check where a value came from instead of taking Assistant's word for it. To validate a page you've built, open a source in Explore mode in Grafana Cloud to run the same query over the same time range, compare it with what the Page shows, and keep digging from there.Pages also build on the access you already have. They work with any existing data connections you have configured in Grafana Cloud, and Grafana's permissions and data source policies still apply to every request. If a page can do something beyond reading data, like sending a Slack message or making an HTTP request, Grafana shows you the destination and values to review before it runs.See what people are buildingEarly internal examples show the range of experiences people are creating with Pages, from business monitoring to release tools and visual storytelling. In this section, we'll link to some of these projects so you can check them out. We've also embedded several of the pages directly into this post so you can interact with them here, too.Run your operationsPages can replace the tab-hopping that comes with triage, audits, and capacity reviews. Each of these examples gathers the data, ranks what matters, and lets you act on it.Triage. Check the health of services across the (fictional) Astronomy Shop and Bank production namespaces. Triage surfaces SLO burn, error and latency regressions, and firing alerts. Pick the most urgent service and open an investigation from the same view.Service health. See which services are burning or have spent their SLO error budget. Select a service to drill into its traffic, error rate, p95 latency, and firing alerts over the time range you choose.Rightsizing. items.title: Break the link between data volume and your observability bill with Adaptive Telemetry
items.summary: In the AI era, where telemetry is generated by every model call, tool invocation, and agent step, organizations need more help than ever when it comes to navigating the economics of observability.For a lot of teams, the default response is a "data diet" of shorter retention, which leaves services or environments out of collection, or basic sampling, which is more guesswork than strategy. Either way, you end up cutting to control the bill, and you risk losing the very data you need during an incident.Your costs shouldn't scale with how much data you ingest. Instead, they should scale with the value you get from it, so you only pay to keep the data that earns its place.That’s what Adaptive Telemetry is built for, and organizations such as Rapid7 are already seeing the results.“Moving to Grafana Cloud and using Adaptive Telemetry cut our metrics costs enough to fund logs and traces as well," says Carl Eastman, Principal Software Engineer, Rapid7. "Our visibility went up while our costs went down, and dashboards and queries are faster and less noisy.” You can already use Adaptive Telemetry for all your observability signals, and we're continuing to build on that foundation so you can get even more precise about which traces you keep, improve your logs economics, and get more from Adaptive Metrics with less toil. Here's how that looks in practice.Keep only the traces that matter, and cut volume by 90% Traces are where the data diet hurts most. Many teams sample with a fixed percentage, which treats a slow checkout request the same as a routine health check. Cut the percentage and your bill drops, but so does the chance that the trace you need is still there when something breaks.Adaptive Traces already handles the hard part (tail sampling) without you running a pipeline. Three newer capabilities make retention even more precise.Automatically keep your most valuable traces, without the policy toilVolumetric sampling gives you a more valuable sample than probabilistic sampling does. It spreads your sampling budget fairly across services and request types, so low-volume services aren't crowded out, and it keeps adjusting as your traffic changes. You set one number (your sampling percentage) without writing complicated policies or tuning them by hand. In Grafana Labs' testing, it delivered about 25% higher information density than probabilistic sampling at the same volume.Keep at least one trace from each footprint, so there’s always something to reference Diversity sampling makes sure you always have something to look at. Every 15 minutes, it stores a unique combination of attributes such as service, route, and status codes. When your environment changes, you don't have to write and update custom sampling logic to catch a new service or code path.Sample aggressively and still retrieve the exact trace you need The ability to query traces dropped by Adaptive Traces is your safety net. Adaptive Traces keeps every dropped trace queryable by trace ID for 24 hours after ingest. If you have the trace ID from a log line, a support ticket, or a testing framework, you can retrieve that specific trace even if Adaptive Traces dropped it. Dropped traces don't appear in search or aggregations, so it's a lookup, not a replacement for sampling the traces you want to search. That's what lets you sample aggressively with confidence.Together, you can use these features to cut trace volume significantly without wondering whether you cut something you needed.Volumetric and diversity sampling, along with the ability to query dropped traces, are all generally available.Improve your logs economics without giving up the data you might needLogs add up fast, and a lot of what you store never gets looked at. Adaptive Logs already finds the log patterns nobody queries and trims them on the way in. Now, two new capabilities help you cut earlier, and with more confidence.Drop unwanted logs at the source and cut egress and network overheadFleet-managed Adaptive Logs uses the same drop rules and exemptions you already use and applies them directly to the collectors you already run, through Fleet Management. Matching logs are filtered out before they ever leave your environment, so you save on egress and network overhead on top of your storage savings. Adaptive Logs creates and keeps the collector pipelines in sync for you, so there's nothing extra to write or maintain. Pattern-based recommendations still run in Grafana Cloud for everything that remains.Keep what you might need, retain it in low-cost storageTeams are understandably cautious about dropping logs. After all, a dropped line can't be recovered, so it's understandable when teams hold back. Archive and replay changes that. Archive routes logs to your own low-cost object storage instead of dropping them. Replay brings them back on demand when you need them for an investigation, an audit, or a compliance request. items.title: Full-stack observability in Grafana Cloud: More connections, richer context, and faster investigations for users and agents
items.summary: Most teams have telemetry from across their stack, but connecting those signals to understand what's happening and how it affects users isn't always easy. Critical context about service dependencies, ownership, and past incidents often lives across tools, runbooks, and conversations between team members.That’s why, today at ObservabilityCON 2026, we’re announcing new capabilities that advance full-stack observability across Grafana Cloud. Powering this experience is the Knowledge Graph, the runtime context layer in Grafana Cloud that brings together your system's components, their relationships, and health insights in one connected view.We're expanding the Knowledge Graph to cover more infrastructure, applications, and user-facing signals, along with a broader range of operational context, including your service catalog, the teams on call, and lessons captured during past incidents. Together, these connections give people and AI agents the same shared context, built on open standards, about how a system fits together, helping them to troubleshoot and find root causes faster. “We've found that the hardest part of an investigation is rarely a lack of data. The challenge is connecting service ownership, dependencies, operational knowledge, and customer impact across a complex ecosystem,” said Neil Wilson, Senior Director of Software Engineering at LexisNexis Risk Solutions. “Entity graph relationships [on the Knowledge Graph] help make those connections visible, giving engineers and AI systems the context they need to move from data to understanding to action."Think of Grafana Cloud as your SRE specialist: whether you work with Grafana Assistant or bring your own agent through gcx, you want that specialized expertise available when you need it, without spending the first half of an investigation reconstructing how everything fits together. That's where we're taking full-stack observability: towards faster, more reliable, and more cost-effective answers, powered by the Knowledge Graph.A connected view of your system: making the full stack even fullerWe're evolving the Knowledge Graph to be a platform capability, available in every stack, where you can curate context across Grafana Cloud.Traditionally, the Knowledge Graph has supported Grafana Cloud Application Observability, Kubernetes Monitoring, Database Observability, and Cloud Provider Observability. These solutions automatically discover their respective entities, such as services, pods, and nodes, and map these entities and their relationships onto the Knowledge Graph. They then monitor entity health and add these insights onto the graph, highlighting everything from deviations from dynamic baselines to configuration changes.Now we're extending that full-stack picture, bringing more of your environment into the Knowledge Graph:Frontend apps (generally available): Frontend Observability maps frontend apps and user-facing signals to the services and infrastructure behind them.Synthetic checks (public preview): Alerts from Synthetic Monitoring checks now appear alongside service health, so you can spot issues and investigate faster.More Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure cloud resources (generally available): Cloud Provider Observability now maps more of your Google Cloud, AWS, and Azure resources for a more complete picture of your cloud infrastructure.AI agents (public preview): Agent Observability maps your AI agents alongside their dependencies, so you can see how they connect to the rest of your system.Microsoft SQL Server databases (private preview): Database Observability now discovers SQL Server databases and maps them automatically.With these updates, you can investigate issues across more of your stack, from a user-facing app to the services, databases, and infrastructure behind it.Go beyond telemetry with richer context in the Knowledge Graph Knowing how your system fits together is important, but to investigate issues effectively, you also need context that’s unique to your organization, including which teams are responsible for which services, how those services support your products and business processes, and what you've learned from past incidents.We're bringing more of that context into the Knowledge Graph, and making it available to both engineering teams and the AI agents they work with every day. Service context: connect services to their owners with Grafana Cloud Service CenterWhile your telemetry describes what’s actually running, a service catalog describes your system in terms your organization understands. Connecting the two gives an investigation a route from a deployed component to the service it belongs to, the team responsible for it, and the guidance they maintain.The new Knowledge Graph integration with Grafana Cloud Service Center, now in private preview, brings these connections onto the graph, so you can see service ownership, on-call schedules, and runbooks alongside the components they support.For example, let’s take Everyday Ch

items.title: Expand what’s possible with Grafana: The Grafana Marketplace is now generally available
items.summary: Earlier this year, we launched the Grafana Marketplace, a platform that gives independent software vendors, systems integrators, and developers in the Grafana community a new way to sell and distribute plugins built for Grafana.The Marketplace builds on our existing plugin catalog by enabling third-party partners and developers to earn revenue from their plugins and invest further in their development. For end users, these paid Marketplace plugins come with guarantees for ongoing updates and support, helping ensure the integrations you rely on remain secure and reliable over time.Since launching the pilot program in April, the Marketplace has grown to include more than 30 custom, partner-backed plugins for high-demand data sources and apps, ranging from cloud cost optimization tools to security solutions from Rubrik and Cisco. Today at ObservabilityCON 2026, we’re excited to share that the Grafana Marketplace is generally available. And to make it easier to explore, any Grafana Cloud user can now trial Marketplace plugins free for 14 days.Why the Marketplace mattersThe Grafana plugin catalog includes more than 300 plugins built and maintained by Grafana Labs, our partners, and the community. This ecosystem gives users more ways to connect Grafana to the tools and data sources they rely on, while giving developers the freedom to extend Grafana for new use cases.We want developers to be inspired to keep building on Grafana, while our users have more options for monitoring their infrastructure and managing their Grafana instances, including apps and data sources for specialized use cases.But building and maintaining a production-grade plugin takes a lot of work. Until recently, independent developers and systems integrators had no direct way to fund that work through the Grafana plugin ecosystem. The Marketplace introduced that commercial model. By giving partners a way to earn revenue from their plugins, they can invest in ongoing development and support while bringing more specialized solutions to Grafana Cloud and Grafana Enterprise users across observability, security, IoT, and beyond. The result is more production-ready data sources and apps reaching the catalog, backed by the ongoing support users need to rely on them.Importantly, the Marketplace adds to our existing plugin ecosystem; it doesn’t replace it. Community and open source plugins remain a core part of Grafana, and developers can continue to build and publish free plugins just as they do today. The Marketplace provides another path for developers who want to sell their plugins and take on the corresponding support and maintenance commitments.Explore the growing Grafana Marketplace Since we launched the pilot, the Marketplace has grown to cover more than 30 high-demand data sources and apps, with options spanning networking, security, storage, virtualization, collaboration, cost management, industrial infrastructure, and more.Below are some examples of the Marketplace plugins available today:Network and security: Cisco Meraki, Rubrik Security Cloud, Zscaler ZIA and ZPA, and Akamai data sources from Crest Data.Storage and virtualization: NetApp ONTAP, Dell PowerScale, and VMware vSphere from Crest Data, and Proxmox VE from Ridgeline Technologies.Productivity and collaboration: SharePoint, Citrix Cloud, Tableau, and Zoom from Crest Data, and end-to-end Microsoft Teams observability from Phenisys.Cost and compute: Kubecost and Nutanix from Integration Plumbers.Industrial infrastructure: Helin Connect Data Hub data source from Helin Data.Manufacturing quality analytics: A full statistical process control (SPC) suite and 3D CAD visualization from KensoBI.Marketplace plugins run inside your own Grafana instance, and Grafana Labs reviews every listing before it goes live. All plugins must be cryptographically signed and must encrypt sensitive data. Partners are contractually obligated to remediate critical vulnerabilities within seven days and high-severity vulnerabilities within 30 days.While Grafana Labs handles billing and payment, support for these plugins comes directly from the partners who built them. We vet every partner and each one is contractually committed to keeping its plugins compatible with supported Grafana versions. Try Marketplace plugins free in Grafana CloudEvery Marketplace plugin comes with a 14-day free trial and full functionality from the first click. Find these plugins in the catalog, or in the Plugins tab of your Grafana Cloud stack, and start a trial.If you're a contracted Grafana Cloud customer, please reach out to your account team to set up your trial. We’d love to hear from youThe Grafana Marketplace is still early, and we want to keep building it the Grafana Labs way: with your input. If a technology you rely on isn't covered yet, reach out at plugins-marketplace@grafana.com.  And if you’re a developer interested in contributing your plugins to the Marketplace, please submit this form.
